title: Log Review & Analysis
description: What to monitor logs for, how a SIEM handles log data from generation to disposal, and continuous monitoring of controls.

nodes.title: Monitor for
nodes.description:
The main things to look for in log data: something broken, unauthorized changes to systems, and signs of a compromise.
- Log what is relevant. Many systems can generate an avalanche of event data, so configure them to log only what matters.
- Review the logs, ideally as close to real time as possible. Finding a significant breach months after it happened is not ideal.
- Look for errors and anomalies.

children.title: Errors
children.description:
Errors show that something is broken and needs to be fixed.
Example: a web server generating many Error 404 (file not found) messages.

children.title: Modification
children.description:
Unauthorized _____ of a system, such as unexpected patching.
Attackers often exploit a vulnerability to break in, install something like a backdoor, then patch the vulnerability behind them. Unauthorized patching of a system may indicate an attacker got in.

children.title: Breaches
children.description:
Signs that an attacker has already compromised a system.
Examples: a system used for cryptocurrency mining, data exfiltration, or an imminent ransomware attack.

nodes.title: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)
nodes.description:
So many devices and systems generate so much log data that finding a problem is like looking for a needle in a haystack. SIEM systems automate many of the logging and monitoring tasks and the analysis.
The SIEM process runs from Generation to Disposal.

children.title: Generation
children.description:
Before data can feed a SIEM, enable logging on devices across the environment so they produce log data.
Almost every system can produce log event data:
- Network devices such as firewalls, routers and switches
- IDS and IPS (Intrusion Detection and Intrusion Prevention Systems)
- Servers, desktops and laptops
- Operating systems
- Applications
- Anti-malware

children.title: Limiting log file size
children.description: Network devices such as firewalls, routers and switches can produce a lot of log data but have very limited onboard storage, so the amount of log data they keep must be capped.

children.title: Circular Overwrite
children.description:
Set a maximum log file size, for example 10 MB or 10,000 lines.
When the log reaches the maximum, writing wraps around to the top of the file and replaces the oldest entries, until it reaches the maximum again. Rinse and repeat.

children.title: Clipping Levels
children.description:
Set a threshold: below it, log nothing; above it, start logging.
Example: one or two failed logins are normal, because everyone mistypes a password. 10, 50 or 10,000 failed attempts in quick succession mean someone is trying to brute force a password.
With the threshold at 3 failed logins, fewer than 3 are not logged; 3 or more are logged.

children.title: Time Stamps
children.description: Every log event needs to record the date and time it happened, so events from different systems can be correlated.

children.title: Consistent
children.description:
Use the same timestamp format on every system, for example year, month, day and a 24-hour clock.
Consistent timestamps make it easier to correlate events from different systems.

children.title: Network Time Protocol (NTP)
children.description:
The clocks of all systems in the environment must be synchronized.
It is very hard to trace how an attacker moved through a network if one system's clock is 3 seconds slow, another is 5 seconds fast, and another's date is set to 1979.
NTP synchronizes all system clocks.

children.title: Transmission
children.description: When any device generates a log event, send the event data to the SIEM in real time.

children.title: Collection / Aggregation
children.description: The SIEM gathers event data from across the environment and combines it in one central system.

children.title: Normalization
children.description: The SIEM cleans up event data from disparate devices, so that all the data and variables are comparable.

children.title: Analysis
children.description:
The SIEM examines the incoming event data to find the needle in the haystack: errors and anomalies.
Techniques include event correlation, statistical models and rules.

children.title: Retention
children.description: The SIEM keeps log event data in long-term storage, for longitudinal analysis and tracking, and to meet contractual or regulatory log retention requirements.

children.title: Disposal
children.description: When event data no longer needs to be kept, destroy it securely and defensibly.

nodes.title: Continuous Monitoring
nodes.description: The organization identifies all its systems and the risks to each one, applies controls to mitigate those risks, then keeps assessing the controls on an ongoing basis to see how effective they are against the ever-changing threat landscape.
